benchmark_type_evidence: We create new datasets for OCR, autocomplete, question answering, semantic parsing, and transliteration, and build on and refine existing datasets for other tasks.
brief_description: XTREME-UP is a multilingual benchmark focusing on user-centric tasks in a scarce-data setting for 88 under-represented languages across 9 key technologies including ASR, OCR, MT, and information access tasks. It standardizes multilingual in-language fine-tuning based on realistic annotation costs (8 hours per language).

datasets.variant_notes: Uses Maestro-U ASR predictions as input, then fine-tunes LMs to improve outputs. Evaluates on 77 under-represented languages.
datasets.translation_method: professional translation — FLEURS recordings are of FLORES-101 sentences translated from English Wikipedia to 101 languages
datasets.annotation_method: speech recordings of translated sentences by native speakers

data_creator_info.evidence: We employ the FLEURS dataset (Conneau et al., 2023) consisting of recordings in 102 languages for sentences from FLORES-101

datasets.source_reference: Conneau et al., 2023 (FLEURS); Goyal et al., 2022 (FLORES-101)
datasets.notes: 77 under-represented languages evaluated; 23 high-resource languages included for training. Sub-sampled to 8h annotation budget per language.

datasets.variant_notes: New dataset created for XTREME-UP focusing on book page transcriptions in 7 under-represented languages.
datasets.annotation_method: human transcription of book pages; annotators transcribed entire pages from public-domain books

data_creator_info.evidence: We create a dataset that aims to fill the gaps in previous work in OCR for ULs... We retrieve books that are in the public domain on Google Books.

datasets.notes: Books domain; includes religious, linguistic, and other public-domain books filtered for quality. 9 training pages per language (~290 lines of output text). Annotation cost: 44.5 min/example (per page).

datasets.variant_notes: Processed from Universal Dependencies treebanks; deduplicated against mC4 to test predictive rather than memorization capabilities.
datasets.annotation_method: derived from existing Universal Dependencies treebanks with automated processing to create autocomplete examples

data_creator_info.evidence: We process high-quality natural language data from Universal Dependencies (de Marneffe et al., 2021), which we deduplicate against mC4

datasets.source_reference: de Marneffe et al., 2021 (Universal Dependencies); Nivre et al., 2020
datasets.notes: 20 under-represented languages + 2 high-resource + English for prototyping. Evaluated with Acc@3. Up to 2,000 training examples per language.

datasets.variant_notes: Extended with Amharic romanizations and Punjabi Shahmukhi transliterations. 30 transliteration tasks across 13 languages.
datasets.annotation_method: human romanization/transliteration by native speakers; Wikipedia sentences romanized by native speakers

data_creator_info.evidence: 10,000 Wikipedia sentences written in the native scripts of the 12 languages were human-romanized by native speakers... Amharic Wikipedia sentences were similarly manually romanized by native speakers; and the Punjabi sentences from the Dakshina dataset were manually transliterated by native speakers to the Shahmukhi script.

datasets.notes: 12 languages from original Dakshina + 1 new (Amharic). 2,000 training sentences per task, ~6,000 test. Covers 3 language families (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Semitic).

datasets.variant_notes: English-to-X translation; half of original dev set repurposed as training set. 93 target languages, 39 ULs evaluated.
datasets.translation_method: professional translation from English (original FLORES-101 creation)

data_creator_info.evidence: The dataset is adapted from FLORES-101 (Goyal et al., 2022), repurposing half of the dataset's original development set as a training set.

datasets.notes: Source data from Wikinews, Wikijunior, and Wikivoyage. 499/498/1012 sentence pairs for train/validation/test. 39 ULs evaluated, 93 total languages.

datasets.variant_notes: Augmented gold passage setting with negative examples from same article and unanswerable questions.
datasets.annotation_method: human annotation — information-seeking questions written without knowing the answer

data_creator_info.evidence: We obtain original questions and passages from TyDi QA (Clark et al., 2020).

datasets.notes: 6 ULs + 3 HLs for in-language QA. Evidence text from Wikipedia. Negative examples added from same article and unanswerable pairs.

datasets.variant_notes: Question in user's language, passage/answer in English. Includes new data in 23 Indic languages via professional translation.
datasets.translation_method: professionally translating questions and answers from existing Indic languages in XOR QA for new Indic languages
datasets.annotation_method: mix of original annotation (TyDi/XOR QA) and professional translation for new Indic languages

data_creator_info.evidence: We use examples from TyDi XOR (Asai et al., 2021) in 7 languages. We additionally collect new data in 23 new Indic languages for cross-lingual QA by professionally translating questions and answers from existing Indic languages in XOR QA.

datasets.source_reference: Asai et al., 2021 (XOR QA); Clark et al., 2020 (TyDi QA)
datasets.notes: 21 ULs + 6 HLs. Translation methodology mitigates English-centric bias by translating from existing Indic languages rather than English.

datasets.variant_notes: Combined MasakhaNER and MasakhaNER 2.0, mapped from CoNLL token format to byte-level spans in raw text. Hausa and Fon subsets excluded due to quality issues.
datasets.annotation_method: human annotation by native speakers (original MasakhaNER datasets); byte-span re-alignment by XTREME-UP authors

data_creator_info.evidence: Both datasets were created by Masakhane. The data is human-annotated and thus higher quality than automatically collected NER datasets.

datasets.source_reference: Adelani et al., 2021 (MasakhaNER); Adelani et al., 2022 (MasakhaNER 2.0)
datasets.notes: 20 African languages. All under-represented. Hausa and Fon excluded from MasakhaNER 2.0 due to annotation quality issues. Lists 18 languages by name but paper states 20 total.

datasets.variant_notes: Extended to 15 new languages via professional translation with localization; 3 additional Indic code-switched variants via PaLM + human verification. Total 20 languages.
datasets.translation_method: professional translation with localization (Western-centric entities replaced with culturally relevant ones); code-switching via PaLM with human verification for 3 Indic languages
datasets.annotation_method: professional translators with localization guidelines; PaLM-generated code-switching with human verification for Indic languages

data_creator_info.evidence: We adapt the test split of MTOP with professional translators/annotators to 15 languages... we collect localized data (i.e., Western-centric entities are replaced with more culturally relevant entities for the target language)

datasets.notes: 9 ULs + 11 HLs. 15 newly translated languages + original 6 MTOP languages (minus overlap) = 20. 3 additional code-switched Indic variants (Hindi-English, Bengali-English, Tamil-English). Max 285 training / 239 dev / 3,669 test per language.

translated.evidence: FLEURS recordings are of FLORES-101 sentences translated from English Wikipedia to 101 languages.

native_annotators.evidence: FLEURS consists of recordings by native speakers of the translated sentences.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Source sentences come from English Wikipedia content.

FLEURS (ASR).annotation_quality_notes: ASR baseline uses Maestro-U with average CER of 8.28% across 102 languages.

translated.evidence: Books in the public domain from Google Books in seven under-represented languages.

native_annotators.evidence: INSUFFICIENT_INFO: Paper does not explicitly confirm annotators were native speakers.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Books are in target languages but many are religious/missionary in origin. Filtering applied for quality.

UL-OCR.annotation_quality_notes: 44.5 minutes per page annotation cost. Baseline Google Vision OCR CER of 11.1%.

translated.evidence: Data from Universal Dependencies treebanks containing naturally occurring text.

native_annotators.evidence: Universal Dependencies treebanks created by linguists and native speakers.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Natural text in each language reflecting natural usage.

Autocomplete (Universal Dependencies).annotation_quality_notes: Deduplicated against mC4. Up to 2,000 training examples per language.

translated.evidence: Wikipedia sentences in native scripts human-romanized. Transliteration, not translation.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Source is Wikipedia in each language; task is script conversion.

Dakshina Transliteration.annotation_quality_notes: 2,000 training / ~6,000 test sentences per task. CER used for evaluation.

translated.evidence: Source data from English Wikinews/Wikijunior/Wikivoyage translated to 93 languages.
Original questions and passages from TyDi QA, natively authored.

native_annotators.evidence: Information-seeking questions written by native speakers.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Natively authored from each language's Wikipedia.

TyDi QA / XOR QA (In-language QA).annotation_quality_notes: Augmented gold passage setting with negatives.

translated.evidence: Original XOR languages have native questions; 23 new Indic languages use professional translation from existing Indic languages.

native_annotators.evidence: Original 7 XOR languages natively authored; 23 Indic languages professionally translated.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Mitigates English-centricity by translating from Indic languages rather than English.

TyDi QA / XOR QA (Cross-language QA).annotation_quality_notes: Cross-language: question in user's language, passage/answer in English.

translated.evidence: Human-annotated NER in 20 African languages from original text.

native_annotators.evidence: Created by Masakhane community of African NLP researchers.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Annotated by African researchers in their native languages.

MasakhaNER-X.annotation_quality_notes: Hausa and Fon excluded due to quality issues. Byte-span re-alignment applied.

translated.evidence: English MTOP adapted via professional translation to 15 languages.

native_annotators.evidence: Professional translators with localization; code-switched data verified by native speakers.

culturally_grounded.evidence: Western-centric entities replaced with culturally relevant ones, but task structure from English MTOP.

MTOP++ (Semantic Parsing).annotation_quality_notes: Two pilots before full annotation. Manual + automatic quality checks.

datasets_from_scratch_no_english_source.evidence: UL-OCR uses public-domain books in target languages. Autocomplete derives from UD treebanks. Dakshina uses Wikipedia in native scripts. TyDi QA collects questions natively. MasakhaNER is human-annotated in African languages.

datasets_translated_from_english.evidence: FLEURS/FLORES-101 translated from English Wikipedia. MTOP++ translated from English MTOP.

details.Autocomplete (Universal Dependencies): Natural text from each language's treebanks.
details.Dakshina Transliteration: Wikipedia content natively in each South Asian language.
details.TyDi QA / XOR QA (In-language QA): Natively authored from each language's Wikipedia.
details.MasakhaNER-X: Human-annotated by African researchers in African languages.
details.MTOP++ (Semantic Parsing): Partial: localized entities replacing Western-centric ones.

all_annotators_native_speakers.evidence: Dakshina: 'human-romanized by native speakers'. MasakhaNER: 'created by Masakhane'. MTOP++: professional translators. OCR/autocomplete annotator nativeness not explicitly confirmed.

annotator_workforce.evidence: Paper lists detailed author contributions but no annotator demographics, compensation, or IRB review.

cultural_flags.english_centricity_notes: Multiple datasets translated from English (FLEURS/FLORES-101, MTOP). Cross-language QA uses English passages. Mitigated by natively-authored datasets (TyDi QA, MasakhaNER, UD), MTOP++ localization, and Indic QA translation from Indic languages rather than English.

geographic_representation.evidence: 88 ULs spanning Africa (20+ via MasakhaNER/FLEURS), South Asia (13 transliteration + 23 Indic QA), Europe (UD autocomplete), Central Asia (Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Tajik, Uyghur). 14 language families represented.
